summary: CYBER-KATAM (Closed-Loop Dynamic Transition-Window Governance & Fiscal-Actuarial Clearing Engine) is a physics-guided, multi-sensor agricultural decision-support system engineered to govern monsoon cropping transitions and evaluate their fiscal-actuarial implications across Banyumas, Central Java. By harmonizing NASA Earth observation products, high-resolution numerical weather forecasts from the Meteomatics API, and localized agronomic constraints onto a hierarchical Uber H3 hexagonal grid, the platform couples sub-surface environmental diagnostics with sequential crop water-balance modeling and multi-objective epsilon-constraint Pareto rotation optimization. Rather than issuing unconstrained black-box predictions, its Integration & Decision Engine enforces a fail-closed governance protocol that synthesizes agro-hydrological suitability, three-tier symbiotic nitrogen accounting, fertilizer subsidy clearing, and agricultural insurance risk assessment into verifiable strategic and 72-hour tactical advisories.
details:
Project Overview

CYBER-KATAM is a modular, multi-scale agro-informatics platform that integrates satellite remote sensing, numerical weather forecasting, process-based crop modeling, and actuarial economics to support climate-resilient farming decisions. Agricultural management in tropical monsoon regimes involves tightly coupled biophysical and socioeconomic dynamics—including root-zone soil moisture variability, canopy thermal stress, bare-fallow soil erosion, stage-specific crop water demand, biological nitrogen fixation, and farm-level financial feasibility—that cannot be resolved through isolated datasets or single-variable indices.

To resolve these interdependencies without sacrificing physical interpretability, CYBER-KATAM processes heterogeneous geospatial inputs across an Uber H3 hexagonal hierarchy through three co-equal analytical modules:

  • Historical & Spatial Modeling: Quantifies sub-surface root-zone water stress (PVRS) and bare-soil degradation hazards (MBSI and BF-EHSI) using multi-sensor NASA observations.
  • Crop Modeling: Evaluates cultivar parameters, sequential FAO-56 soil water balances (ETo and ETc), phenological calendars, multi-season Pareto crop rotations, and 72-hour tactical field advisories driven by the Meteomatics Weather API.
  • Economic, Fiscal & Actuarial Modeling: Estimates three-tier biological nitrogen fixation carryover, regional fertilizer subsidy clearing (S_net), farm gross margins, and agricultural insurance risk reductions (AUTP).

Outputs from these modules converge within an overarching Integration & Decision Engine, which audits data provenance and parameter completeness before rendering actionable insights through a dual-persona web application for farmers, extension officers (PPL), and policymakers. Piloted across the topographically diverse agro-ecosystem of Banyumas Regency, Central Java, Indonesia, the architecture is designed for regional scalability while operating strictly as an explainable, human-in-the-loop decision-support framework rather than a replacement for local agronomic verification.

Problem Statement

Monsoon-dependent rice ecosystems face structural vulnerabilities during inter-seasonal transitions, where single-variable monitoring fails to capture compounding agronomic and financial risks (Huang et al., 2025). Conventional optical vegetation indices exhibit a 9-to-14-day physiological lag behind sub-surface root-zone moisture depletion, masking early stomatal closure until irreversible yield penalties occur (Fang et al., 2022). Conversely, leaving fields bare (bera) during dry transitions induces clay desiccation cracking, evaporative moisture loss, and severe sheet erosion upon the onset of high-intensity monsoon precipitation (Pereira et al., 2020; Shafiei et al., 2026). CYBER-KATAM specifically targets seven systemic bottlenecks:

  • Fragmented integration across satellite hydro-climatology, crop physiology, and agricultural policy metrics.
  • Unresolved spatial heterogeneity in root-zone moisture and topographic drainage across micro-parcels.
  • High uncertainty in short-term meteorological forcings and field-level irrigation availability.
  • Computational complexity in evaluating multi-season crop sequences against competing ecological trade-offs.
  • Accelerated soil organic carbon depletion and rainfall-driven erosion during unplanted fallow windows.
  • Unquantified carryover of biological nitrogen fixation into subsequent chemical fertilizer displacement.
  • Disconnected assessment between field-level agronomic transitions, state fertilizer subsidies, and crop insurance liabilities.

Project Objectives

  • Harmonize multi-sensor NASA Earth observation products, localized agronomic registries, and Meteomatics numerical weather forecasts within a unified spatial framework.
  • Quantify sub-surface physiological water stress and bare-soil degradation hazards across heterogeneous agricultural terrains.
  • Evaluate stage-specific crop water requirements, phenological calendars, and multi-season rotation sequences.
  • Drive 72-hour tactical field advisories using sequential forward water-balance stepping.
  • Formulate a rigorous accounting framework for symbiotic nitrogen fixation, fiscal subsidy clearing, and agricultural insurance risk.
  • Synthesize multi-domain model outputs through a single canonical Pareto optimization and decision-validation workflow.
  • Deliver transparent, role-tailored visual analytics via an interactive geospatial web application.
  • Enforce explicit data provenance tracking and fail-closed abstention protocols to prevent unsupported operational claims.

System Architecture

CYBER-KATAM uses a modular architecture consisting of data sources, data processing, three main modeling modules, an Integration & Decision Engine, and a web application

Data Processing & Spatial Analysis

The data processing layer prepares heterogeneous inputs for the modeling modules. It performs data validation, unit normalization, temporal alignment, spatial processing, and H3 indexing where applicable.

Modeling Modules

The system contains three principal modeling modules:

  1. Historical & Spatial Modeling: Analyzes environmental conditions, satellite-derived indicators, vegetation conditions, bare-soil exposure, and spatial hazards.
  2. Crop Modeling: Evaluates crop parameters, water requirements, crop suitability, planting calendars, crop rotation alternatives, and short-term crop management advisories.
  3. Economic, Fiscal & Actuarial Modeling: Evaluates potential fertilizer displacement, economic feasibility, subsidy-related scenarios, and agricultural insurance risks.

External Weather Forecast Integration

Weather forecast information is retrieved from the Meteomatics Weather API and processed as an external data input.

The retrieved forecast is used by the Crop Modeling module, especially the Tactical Crop Advisory component, and can also be consumed by the Integration & Decision Engine.

Integration & Decision Engine

This layer combines the outputs of the three modeling modules and relevant external weather information. It evaluates whether sufficient information is available before producing decision-support outputs.

Agricultural Decision Support & Web Application

The resulting information is organized into agricultural insights and recommendations, then presented through the CYBER-KATAM web application.

Data Sources and Resources

NASA and Satellite Earth Observation Products

CYBER-KATAM ingests six primary NASA remote sensing datasets processed via Google Earth Engine to characterize agro-hydrological states (Huang et al., 2025; Kumar et al., 2025):

  • NASA SMAP L4 Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP): Provides 3-hourly surface and root-zone soil moisture (0–100 cm) to establish sub-surface water-stress baselines.
  • NASA MODIS / ECOSTRESS Land Surface Temperature (MOD11A / ECO_L2T_LSTE): Supplies canopy thermal emissions and Evaporative Stress Index (ESI) inputs to detect stomatal closure.
  • NASA GPM IMERG (V07): Delivers half-hourly precipitation rates for effective rainfall partitioning and 95th-percentile kinetic erosivity modeling (Sujakhu et al., 2026).
  • NASA HLS v2.0 (Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel): Offers 30 m surface reflectance across Red, NIR, SWIR1, and SWIR2 bands to derive vegetation and bare-soil indices.
  • NASA SRTM (SRTMGL1): Provides 30 m digital elevation data to compute terrain slope (θ_SRTM) and surface hydrological connectivity.
  • NASA POWER Agro-Climatology: Supplies agro-meteorological radiation and temperature series for baseline reference evapotranspiration (ETo) calculations.

External Weather Forecast Data

Short-range meteorological forcings are retrieved via the Meteomatics Weather API (NASA Space Apps Challenge Partner), a RESTful service providing coordinate-specific hourly and daily forecasts for precipitation, air temperature, wind speed, and solar radiation.

Agricultural Registry and Scientific References

Agronomic parameterization is grounded in the FAO-56 Crop Evapotranspiration standard (Allen et al., 1998; Pereira et al., 2020) and mapped across Uber H3 hexagonal grids and Leaflet web cartography. The initial crop registry encompasses four regionally significant cultivars:

  • Rice (Oryza sativa cv. Inpari 32): A high-yielding irrigated paddy cultivar (~110 days) resistant to bacterial leaf blight, serving as the primary monsoon staple (Purbiati et al., 2024).
  • Soybean (Glycine max cv. Anjasmoro): A lodging-resistant, large-seeded tropical legume (~83 days) capable of symbiotic Bradyrhizobium nitrogen fixation (Adie et al., 2020).
  • Mungbean (Vigna radiata cv. Vima-1): A synchronously maturing, drought-tolerant short-duration legume (~58 days) suited for water-constrained transition windows (Mau, 2017; Sosiawan et al., 2021).
  • Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor cv. Suri 3): A deep-rooting, low-water-demand cereal evaluated for dry-season biomass and grain production (Widodo et al., 2023).

To maintain scientific integrity, the registry strictly differentiates generic reference parameters (e.g., standard FAO crop coefficients) from locally calibrated field measurements in Banyumas.

Technical Stack

The computational backend is implemented in Python (NumPy, Pandas) using standardized JSON/GeoJSON data contracts, while the interactive frontend is built with React, JavaScript, Uber H3, and Leaflet.

Data Processing and Spatial Framework

Because satellite products and numerical weather models operate at disparate spatial footprints (30 m to 10 km) and temporal cadences, the data processing pipeline executes an eight-stage harmonization workflow: raw ingestion, quality-assurance filtering, unit and nomenclature standardization, temporal alignment, boundary clipping, Uber H3 hexagonal indexing, metadata provenance tagging, and schema validation.

By indexing all layers onto hierarchical H3 hexagonal cells, CYBER-KATAM co-locates soil moisture, canopy temperature, spectral reflectance, slope, crop suitability, and socioeconomic attributes within uniform spatial units. Crucially, spatial indexing is not treated as physical resolution enhancement; coarse satellite footprints mapped onto finer H3 cells retain explicit scale-discrepancy error bounds rather than being misrepresented as direct point measurements.

Modeling Methodology

CYBER-KATAM eschews monolithic black-box machine learning in favor of transparent biophysical equations, rule-based agronomic evaluators, and deterministic multi-objective optimization.

1. Historical & Spatial Modeling

This module quantifies sub-surface water deficits and bare-fallow environmental hazards across agricultural cells.

Pre-Visual Root-Stress Score (PVRS) To overcome the 9-to-14-day optical lag of chlorophyll degradation, PVRS couples Evaporative Stress Index (ESI), Land Surface Temperature (LST), and root-zone soil moisture (SM_root) anomalies against optical Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) baselines (Fang et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2023):

Plaintext

S_physio = w1 * ((μ_ESI - ESI) / σ_ESI)
+ w2 * ((LST - μ_LST) / σ_LST)
+ w3 * ((μ_SM - SM_root) / σ_SM)

S_visual = (μ_NDVI - NDVI) / σ_NDVI

PVRS = 1 / (1 + exp(-(S_physio - γ * S_visual)))

Here, μ and σ denote historical decadal means and standard deviations, parameterized with weights w1 = 0.35, w2 = 0.35, w3 = 0.30, and optical lag penalty γ = 0.50. High PVRS values flag incipient stomatal closure while foliage remains optically green, subject to local baseline calibration.

Modified Bare Soil Index (MBSI) and Bare-Field Environmental Hazard and Stress Index (BF-EHSI) To evaluate fallow-period soil exposure using HLS 30 m reflectance, the system computes MBSI and applies a bounded linear transformation to estimate bare-soil fraction b_it within [0, 1] (Shafiei et al., 2026):

Plaintext

MBSI = (SWIR1 - SWIR2 - NIR) / (SWIR1 + SWIR2 + NIR)

b_it = clip((MBSI + 0.15) / 0.45, 0, 1)

Instantaneous fallow hazard (BF-EHSI) and cumulative seasonal degradation risk (D_i) integrate thermal exposure, SRTM slope (θ_SRTM), and bias-corrected 95th-percentile GPM rainfall intensity (R_GPM,95th) (Xu et al., 2024; Sujakhu et al., 2026):

Plaintext

BF-EHSI = b_it * [α * (LST_ECOSTRESS / LST_crit) + β * tan(θ_SRTM) * (R_GPM,95th / R_norm)]

D_i = Σ [b_it * k_i * c_it * e_it * Δt]

Here, k_i, c_it, and e_it represent soil erodibility, topographic surface connectivity, and rainfall kinetic erosivity over time step Δt, respectively.

2. Crop Modeling

The Crop Modeling engine comprises six sub-modules: Crop Parameter Registry, Crop Water Modeling, Crop Suitability, Crop Calendar, Strategic Crop Rotation Modeling, and Tactical Crop Advisory.

Crop Parameter Registry & Water Balance Modeling Every cultivar parameter is stored with explicit unit, bibliographic source, and provenance status (OBSERVED, STANDARD, PROXY, DERIVED, SIMULATED, ASSUMED, or MISSING), preventing silent fallback to arbitrary defaults. Crop water demand follows the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ETo) and stage-specific crop coefficient (Kc) formulation (Allen et al., 1998; Pereira et al., 2020; Anupoju et al., 2024), while root-zone soil water storage (S_t) is updated via a sequential forward mass-balance equation across forecast horizons (H+1 -> H+2 -> H+3):

Plaintext

ETo = [0.408 * Δ * (Rn - G) + γ * (900 / (T + 273)) * u2 * (es - ea)]
/ [Δ + γ * (1 + 0.34 * u2)]

ETc = Kc * ETo

S_t = S_(t-1) + P_eff,t + I_t - ETc,t - RO_t - DP_t

This sequential formulation accounts for effective precipitation (P_eff,t), irrigation (I_t), surface runoff (RO_t), and deep percolation (DP_t) to isolate net irrigation requirements from gross ETc.

Strategic Crop Rotation & Tactical Advisory A rule-based candidate generator enumerates feasible multi-season crop sequences against phenological duration, soil drainage (K_sat), and water-supply constraints. Eligible sequences are evaluated via an epsilon-constraint multi-objective Pareto optimizer that maximizes chemical nitrogen fertilizer displacement (N_displaced), soil organic carbon accrual (ΔSOC), and brown planthopper suppression (-BPH_burden):

Plaintext

Maximize:
f(x) = [N_displaced(x), ΔSOC(x), -BPH_burden(x)]

Subject to:
ΔSOC(x) >= ε1
BPH_burden(x) <= ε2

Optimization is further bounded by farmer subsistence net margin, seasonal water supply, minimum legume root-zone hydraulic conductivity (K_sat), and maximum erosion tolerance (D_i). Candidates lacking verified optimization metrics are excluded from Pareto ranking. Concurrently, the Tactical Crop Advisory consumes 72-hour Meteomatics forecasts and spatial indices (BF-EHSI, soil saturation) to issue short-term planting, irrigation, fertilization, drainage, harvest, and fallow-cover instructions—abstaining automatically whenever essential inputs are absent.

3. Economic, Fiscal & Actuarial Modeling

This module translates field-level agronomic transitions into macro-fiscal and actuarial scenario assessments.

Three-Tier Nitrogen Accounting Because grain harvest exports a substantial fraction of legume nitrogen—often yielding negative partial soil N balances if root residues and fertilizer-use efficiency are ignored (Ciampitti & Salvagiotti, 2018; Zambon et al., 2023; Wysokinski et al., 2024)—CYBER-KATAM implements a three-tier accounting structure parameterized by tropical nodulation and 15N isotope literature (Kihara et al., 2011; Ratajczak et al., 2024; Zahoor et al., 2026):

Plaintext

Tier 1 — Gross Biological Nitrogen Fixation:
N_bio = Biomass * Tissue_N * Ndfa

Tier 2 — Potentially Retained Nitrogen:
N_retained = N_bio * (1 - f_harvest) * (1 - f_denit - f_leach) * f_mineralization

Tier 3 — Potential Chemical Fertilizer Displacement:
ΔN_chem = min(N_retained / (0.46 * NUE), Urea_recommended)

Here, 0.46 denotes the stoichiometric nitrogen fraction of urea and NUE represents cereal nitrogen-use efficiency (Fageria, 2014), modulated by nitrate leaching losses (f_leach) and waterlogging-induced nodule impairment (Maekawa et al., 2011; Meng et al., 2024; Khalil et al., 2026).

Fiscal Subsidy Clearing, Economic Feasibility & Agricultural Insurance Risk Assessment Potential regional fertilizer subsidy implications (S_net) across H3 clusters and farm-level gross margins are modeled by offsetting gross urea displacement savings against extension (C_extension), seed/inoculant transition (C_transition), and verification (C_verification) costs:

Plaintext

S_net = Σ [A_k * a_k * ΔN_chem,k * s_N] - (C_extension + C_transition + C_verification)

Revenue = Yield * Selling_Price
Gross_Margin = Revenue - Production_Cost

Similarly, the actuarial sub-module evaluates how pre-visual drought mitigation (PVRS) and non-host legume rotation windows (interrupting the 24.7-day pre-adult cycle of monophagous Nilaparvata lugens while accounting for macropterous recolonization; EFSA Panel on Plant Health et al., 2023; Naik et al., 2026) alter tail-risk claim probabilities under Indonesia's Asuransi Usaha Tani Padi (AUTP) framework (IJRTE, 2019). In the absence of audited sub-district RDKK subsidy ledgers and historical Jasindo claim micro-data, all fiscal, actuarial, and gross-margin outputs are explicitly badged as scenario simulations rather than realized budget savings.

External Weather Forecast Integration

Rather than training an indigenous numerical weather prediction model, CYBER-KATAM ingests operational 72-hour forecasts via the Meteomatics Weather API. The ingestion pipeline executes a standardized six-step sequence: querying coordinate- and time-specific meteorological parameters, retrieving JSON payloads, validating schema integrity, normalizing variables into canonical ForecastBundle and ForecastDay data structures, routing forcings to the Crop Modeling and Decision Engines, and driving sequential H+1 to H+3 water-balance and tactical advisory rules. While Meteomatics supplies raw atmospheric forcings, all agro-hydrological partitioning and operational gating reside within CYBER-KATAM.

Integration & Decision Engine

Acting as the central governance layer, the Integration & Decision Engine synthesizes spatial stress indicators (PVRS, BF-EHSI), crop suitability and sequential water-balance states, Pareto-ranked rotation candidates, fiscal-actuarial metrics, and 72-hour weather forecasts into a unified grid_cell_contract.json payload.

To eliminate AI hallucination and unsupported policy claims, the engine enforces a strict fail-closed governance protocol bounded by analytical Lipschitz error propagation:

  • Validated Advisory (ACTIVE_RECOMMENDATION): Emitted only when sensor quality gates pass, spatial uncertainty bounds remain within tolerance, and required model inputs are complete.
  • Conditional Output or Governed Abstention (ABSTAIN_FIELD_AUDIT_REQUIRED): Triggered automatically whenever severe cloud cover, coarse-to-fine spatial support discrepancies, or missing local parameters exceed confidence thresholds.
  • Explicit Provenance Tagging: Every output variable carries an immutable evidence status (OBSERVED, STANDARD, PROXY, DERIVED, SIMULATED, ASSUMED, or MISSING), mandating physical inspection by agricultural extension officers (Penyuluh Pertanian Lapangan / PPL) before field execution.

Explainability and Human Verification

Every parcel-level recommendation is accompanied by a structured Four-Block Explainable AI (XAI) Decision Certificate designed for transparent human audit:

  • Evidence (why_suggested): Cites exact satellite and meteorological metrics (e.g., SMAP root-zone moisture, ECOSTRESS thermal anomalies, and effective seasonal water supply) driving the diagnosis.
  • Expected Benefits (multi_benefits): Quantifies projected irrigation savings, conservative vs. simulated urea displacement credits, and pest-cycle interruption duration.
  • Information Gaps (information_gaps): Explicitly discloses unmeasured micro-variables—such as localized farm-gate prices, soil pH, tertiary canal sedimentation, and historical sub-district insurance claims.
  • Local Risks & Verification Gates (local_risks_and_gates): Specifies mandatory human-in-the-loop field checks for farmers and PPL extension officers, such as verifying root-zone drainage (K_sat >= 35 mm/day) to prevent Bradyrhizobium nodule asphyxiation.

Innovation and Creativity

CYBER-KATAM advances agricultural decision support by unifying six multidisciplinary innovations within a single auditable architecture:

  • Coupling thermal-microwave root-zone stress detection (PVRS) and bare-fallow degradation integrals (BF-EHSI) with cultivar-specific agronomic thresholds.
  • Harmonizing multi-resolution satellite observations and socioeconomic data across hierarchical Uber H3 hexagonal grids.
  • Formulating multi-season crop rotation as a constrained multi-objective Pareto optimization problem balancing soil carbon, nitrogen, pest ecology, and farm income.
  • Driving sequential forward soil water-balance calculations with live 72-hour Meteomatics weather forecasts.
  • Bridging plot-level legume agronomy with macro-level state fertilizer subsidy clearing and AUTP crop insurance risk sensitivity.
  • Embedding explicit data provenance vocabularies and fail-closed abstention gates directly into the runtime contract.

Intended Impact

CYBER-KATAM delivers tailored decision intelligence across three primary stakeholder tiers:

  • Farmers & Water-User Associations (P3A): Provides early pre-visual drought warnings, water-feasible cultivar alternatives (e.g., switching from high-water secondary rice to short-duration Vima-1 mungbean or Anjasmoro soybean), and 72-hour operational advisories for irrigation and fertilization timing.
  • Agricultural Extension Officers (PPL): Supplies spatially explicit vulnerability maps and structured field-verification checklists to prioritize on-ground inspections across high-risk H3 cells.
  • Policymakers & Agricultural Insurers: Offers a transparent analytical sandbox to evaluate regional water conservation, potential chemical fertilizer displacement under different adoption scenarios, and agro-ecological mitigation of crop failure liabilities.

Limitations and Future Development

To transition CYBER-KATAM from a proof-of-concept architecture to an operational recommendation system, six structural limitations are explicitly documented and targeted for future development:

  • Spatial Scale Discrepancies: Coarse microwave and precipitation footprints (SMAP 9 km, GPM 10 km) mapped onto H3 cells do not constitute direct plot-scale sensors and require validated physical downscaling and in-situ soil moisture calibration.
  • Agronomic Parameter Calibration: Several crop coefficients, rooting depths, and soil organic carbon responses currently rely on literature proxies or scenario constants rather than multi-season cultivar trials in Banyumas.
  • Local Socioeconomic & Actuarial Micro-Data: Realized fiscal and insurance evaluations require verified sub-district fertilizer allocation records (e-RDKK), localized farm-gate price series, and historical AUTP claim ledgers.
  • Separation of Forecast and Observation Regimes: Numerical weather forecasts from Meteomatics carry inherent horizon-dependent uncertainty and must remain analytically distinct from historical satellite observations.
  • Strict Runtime Contract Enforcement: Full production deployment requires completing all modular evaluators and enforcing automated fail-closed abstention whenever mandatory registry fields are MISSING.
  • Future Roadmap: Next phases prioritize automated GEE/Meteomatics ingestion pipelines, field calibration with local university and extension partners in Banyumas, and end-to-end runtime integration of the canonical Pareto and XAI contract engines.
